entities.name: Montanus of Phrygia
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Montanus of Phrygia, a pivotal figure in early Christian history, emerged around 170 CE in Pepuza, Phrygia, as the founder of Montanism, a prophetic movement that challenged the nascent institutional structures of the Great Church. Claiming to be a mouthpiece for the Paraclete, or Holy Spirit, Montanus, alongside his female prophetesses Prisca and Maximilla, preached an imminent second coming of Christ and a renewed emphasis on spiritual gifts, ecstatic prophecy, and rigorous asceticism. His teachings sparked a profound schism, forcing the developing orthodox church to define its understanding of divine inspiration, ecclesiastical authority, and the canon of scripture against a backdrop of fervent charismatic revival.

Montanus's ministry commenced in Ardabau, Phrygia, characterized by ecstatic utterances delivered in a state of prophetic possession, which followers believed to be direct messages from God. He and his prophetesses called for a stricter moral code, including longer fasts, celibacy, and a rejection of second marriages, anticipating the New Jerusalem to descend upon Pepuza. This emphasis on continuing prophecy and a more demanding spiritual life resonated deeply with some Christians disillusioned by what they perceived as the growing worldliness and hierarchical ossification of the mainstream church. His movement rapidly gained adherents across Anatolia, North Africa, and Rome, attracting both common believers and notable intellectuals.
